clinicalPearls: A malignant tumour of vascular (endothelial) origin that classically affects the scalp and face of elderly patients
Presents deceptively as a bruise-like violaceous patch or plaque that fails to resolve, often with ill-defined margins and later nodularity or bleeding
Three main clinical settings are idiopathic head-and-neck disease in the elderly, post-irradiation angiosarcoma, and lymphoedema-associated Stewart-Treves syndrome
Stewart-Treves syndrome arises in chronically lymphoedematous limbs, historically after mastectomy with axillary clearance
Histology shows irregular anastomosing vascular channels dissecting collagen, lined by atypical endothelial cells, with variable solid and epithelioid areas
Endothelial markers such as CD31, ERG, and often the lymphatic marker D2-40 confirm the diagnosis; MYC amplification supports radiation- and lymphoedema-associated forms
Wide surgical excision with radiotherapy is the mainstay, but multifocal subclinical spread makes clear margins difficult and recurrence common
reference.pathophysiology: Cutaneous angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignancy of endothelial-cell origin in which atypical cells form irregular, anastomosing vascular channels that dissect through dermal collagen and infiltrate widely. Several predisposing contexts are recognised: chronic ultraviolet and actinic damage of the head and neck in the elderly; prior therapeutic irradiation; and long-standing lymphoedema, as in Stewart-Treves syndrome following axillary node clearance, where amplification of the MYC oncogene is characteristic in radiation- and lymphoedema-associated tumours. The neoplastic endothelium retains vascular differentiation, expressing markers such as CD31 and ERG, but grows in a diffuse, often multifocal fashion with extensive subclinical spread that underlies the high rates of local recurrence and early haematogenous metastasis, particularly to lung.
additionalDifferentials: Bruise or haematoma (for the early patch stage)
Squamous or basal cell carcinoma of the scalp
Benign vascular lesions such as haemangioma or pyogenic granuloma
Cellulitis or rosacea (for facial erythematous change)
additionalInvestigations: Incisional biopsy, often multiple, given ill-defined and multifocal spread
Histopathology demonstrating anastomosing atypical vascular channels
Immunohistochemistry for endothelial markers (CD31, ERG) and D2-40, plus MYC assessment
Cross-sectional and chest imaging to assess local extent and pulmonary metastasis
Mapping biopsies to define subclinical margins before surgery
Multidisciplinary sarcoma-team assessment for combined surgery and radiotherapy
redFlags: A persistent bruise-like scalp or facial lesion in an elderly patient that does not resolve
New vascular tumour arising in a chronically lymphoedematous limb (Stewart-Treves)
Cutaneous vascular malignancy within a previously irradiated field
Rapid growth, ulceration, or bleeding of an ill-defined violaceous plaque
reference.prognosis: Cutaneous angiosarcoma has a poor prognosis with high rates of local recurrence and early metastasis, particularly to the lungs; extensive subclinical spread frequently precludes clear surgical margins, and larger tumour size and head-and-neck or metastatic disease predict worse survival.
pitfalls: Dismissing an early bruise-like lesion as a simple contusion or rosacea and delaying biopsy
Underestimating margins because of diffuse multifocal subclinical spread
Failing to consider angiosarcoma in a chronically lymphoedematous limb or previously irradiated site
Not obtaining endothelial immunohistochemistry when the tumour is poorly differentiated or epithelioid
management: Wide surgical resection with clear margins is preferred for localized resectable disease, though multifocal subclinical spread makes clear margins difficult and local recurrence common
Lymphoedema-associated (Stewart-Treves) angiosarcoma poses particular surgical challenges due to poor wound healing in the chronically lymphoedematous limb, sometimes limiting limb-sparing options
Radiotherapy is used as an adjunct to surgery to reduce local recurrence, or as a primary modality when resection is not feasible
Most localized disease is treated with combined surgery plus radiotherapy rather than surgery alone, given the tendency toward multifocal subclinical spread
Angiosarcoma retains relative sensitivity to anthracycline-based chemotherapy and taxanes compared with most other soft tissue sarcomas
Systemic therapy is reserved for unresectable, extensively multifocal, or metastatic disease, including the high rate of hematogenous spread to lung
Antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors and VEGF-pathway-directed agents have shown activity given the vascular origin of the tumor and findings such as KDR mutation and MYC/FLT4 amplification
A beta-blocker (propranolol) combined with metronomic vinblastine-based chemotherapy is an emerging approach reported to produce responses in inoperable disease, not yet an established standard

Immune checkpoint blockade (PD-1 plus CTLA-4 antibody combinations) is under investigation, with reported responses particularly in head-and-neck cutaneous angiosarcoma, which tends to carry higher tumor mutational burden

Sequential systemic therapy in advanced disease typically starts with an anthracycline- or taxane-based regimen, followed by antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors or checkpoint blockade in later lines
Prognosis is generally poor, with worse outcomes associated with older age, greater tumor depth, and larger tumor size
Multicentric head-and-neck disease in elderly patients tends to progress relentlessly locally, with risk of ulceration, infection, and metastasis, warranting close surveillance
Follow-up should include regular skin and field examination for local recurrence plus periodic imaging for pulmonary and other distant metastases

Prompt referral to a sarcoma multidisciplinary team is warranted for any suspected or confirmed case, with early involvement of reconstructive/limb-salvage surgery for lymphoedema-associated or limb-sparing cases, and referral to sarcoma medical oncology or clinical trials for metastatic, unresectable, or recurrent disease

Multiple incisional biopsies; CD31 and ERG staining; chest and local imaging
Does histology show anastomosing atypical vascular channels with endothelial markers?
Consider Kaposi sarcoma, melanoma or a benign vascular lesion
Wide surgical resection with clear margins where feasible
Adjunct radiotherapy to reduce local recurrence
